mechanisms.title: Iron: absorption, transport and storage
mechanisms.lead: Dietary iron enters a tightly regulated recycling system. The gut supplies new iron; recycled red blood cells supply much of the iron used each day.

nodes.name: Dietary iron
nodes.role: Iron released from food reaches the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

nodes.name: Enterocyte
nodes.role: An absorptive cell takes up iron and can retain it in ferritin.

nodes.name: Ferroportin
nodes.role: The exporter releases iron from enterocytes and iron-recycling cells.

nodes.name: Transferrin-bound iron
nodes.role: Transferrin carries iron to tissues, including bone marrow.

nodes.name: Marrow and recycling
nodes.role: Marrow makes red cells; macrophages recover iron from ageing red cells.

nodes.name: Hepcidin
nodes.role: This liver hormone reduces the number of active ferroportin exporters.

steps.title: Crossing the lining
steps.text: Iron enters an enterocyte before export into blood. A dose swallowed is not the same quantity as a dose absorbed.

steps.title: Transport and reuse
steps.text: Transferrin delivers iron to tissues. Recycling cells return recovered iron through ferroportin, connecting red-cell turnover to the circulating pool.

steps.title: The regulatory brake
steps.text: Hepcidin binds ferroportin and removes it from the cell surface. IL-6 during inflammation can raise hepcidin and reduce circulating iron.

measurements.name: Serum iron
measurements.text: The iron circulating in the blood sample at that time; it varies across the day.

measurements.name: Transferrin saturation
measurements.text: The percentage of transferrin binding capacity occupied by iron: serum iron ÷ total iron-binding capacity × 100, using matching units.

measurements.name: Ferritin
measurements.text: A marker of iron stores that also rises during inflammation. Read alongside the blood count and inflammatory context.

measurements.name: Hepcidin
measurements.text: A regulatory measurement used in research and some specialist settings; it describes control of export rather than the size of iron stores.

mechanisms.title: Serotonin: digestion, sensation and gut–brain signals
mechanisms.lead: The gut uses serotonin to turn what it senses into movement, secretion and signals to the brain. It works within a two-way network of nerves, immune messages, hormones and microbial chemistry.

nodes.name: Tryptophan
nodes.role: Dietary tryptophan supplies both peripheral and brain serotonin synthesis. Tryptophan crosses the blood–brain barrier; serotonin itself does not meaningfully cross it.

nodes.name: Enterochromaffin cells
nodes.role: These specialised lining cells make most intestinal serotonin using TPH1. Chemical and mechanical cues trigger release. A smaller population of enteric neurons makes serotonin using TPH2.

nodes.name: Released serotonin
nodes.role: Serotonin activates nearby receptors involved in movement, fluid and electrolyte secretion, sensation and immune responses. Its effect depends on the receptor and tissue.

nodes.name: Enteric and sensory nerves
nodes.role: Enteric circuits coordinate digestive reflexes. Serotonin can also activate receptors on sensory fibres, including vagal afferents that relay gut information toward the brainstem.

nodes.name: Platelet uptake
nodes.role: Platelets take up peripheral serotonin through SERT and store it. On activation they release it into vascular, clotting and inflammatory responses. This circulating reservoir has a different destination from serotonin made inside the brain.

nodes.name: Microbial metabolites
nodes.role: Products of microbial metabolism influence enterochromaffin-cell activity.

steps.title: The gut makes and senses
steps.text: About 90–95% of the body’s serotonin is produced in the intestine, mostly by enterochromaffin cells. These host cells respond to the intestinal environment; microbial metabolites can regulate their synthesis. In the gut, serotonin coordinates digestive and sensory functions.

steps.title: A chemical signal becomes a nerve message
steps.text: Released serotonin activates nearby sensory receptors, including 5-HT3 receptors on vagal fibres. The chemical acts near its release site; nerve activity carries information onward to the brainstem. Enteric circuits also use these signals to organise movement, secretion and sensation.

steps.title: Blood, platelets and the brain
steps.text: Some gut serotonin enters blood and is collected by platelets, which release it when activated. Brain neurons make their own serotonin from tryptophan using TPH2. The gut influences brain activity through nerve signals, precursor metabolism, immunity and other microbial products; those connections do not require circulating serotonin to enter the brain.

measurements.name: Blood serotonin
measurements.text: Sample type matters: platelets contain much of the serotonin measured in whole blood. A blood result does not measure brain serotonin.

measurements.name: Tissue synthesis and release
measurements.text: TPH1 expression, tissue serotonin and release assays describe different parts of the process.

mechanisms.title: Bile acids: digestion, recycling and signalling
mechanisms.lead: Bile acids help absorb fats, circulate between intestine and liver, and act as chemical signals. Microbes reshape this circulating mixture.

nodes.name: Liver bile acids
nodes.role: The liver makes primary bile acids and secretes them into bile.

nodes.name: Digestive bile pool
nodes.role: Bile acids participate in fat digestion and absorption.

nodes.name: Microbial transformations
nodes.role: Deconjugation and further transformations alter the bile-acid mixture.

nodes.name: Ileal uptake
nodes.role: Most bile acids return through the portal circulation.

nodes.name: FXR → FGF19
nodes.role: An intestinal feedback signal regulates liver synthesis.

nodes.name: Immune receptors
nodes.role: Specific bile-acid derivatives influence immune-cell differentiation.

steps.title: Changing the mixture
steps.text: Microbial bile salt hydrolases remove conjugated groups. Other enzymes produce secondary bile acids, changing the pool available for uptake and signalling.

steps.title: Closing the loop
steps.text: Ileal uptake returns bile acids to the liver. Intestinal FXR signalling induces FGF19, feeding back on liver synthesis.

steps.title: Beyond fat digestion
steps.text: Distinct derivatives can affect immune cells differently. The experimental T-cell results concern particular molecules and cell settings.

measurements.name: Bile-acid profiles
measurements.text: Blood or stool profiling identifies a mixture of primary, secondary and conjugated molecules; the sample location changes what is observed.

measurements.name: FGF19
measurements.text: A circulating feedback hormone with a pronounced meal-related rhythm.

mechanisms.title: Fibre to short-chain fatty acids
mechanisms.lead: Microbes turn otherwise inaccessible carbohydrates into fuel and signals. Much of this chemistry depends on exchanges between different organisms.

nodes.name: Fermentable fibre
nodes.role: Plant carbohydrates and resistant starch supply microbial substrates.

nodes.name: Primary degraders
nodes.role: Organisms break down complex carbohydrates and release fermentation products.

nodes.name: Acetate and lactate
nodes.role: Products made by one organism become substrates for another.

nodes.name: Butyrate producers
nodes.role: Cross-feeding supports butyrate production.

nodes.name: Colonocytes
nodes.role: These cells consume butyrate as an energy source.

nodes.name: Portal and systemic pools
nodes.role: Acetate, propionate and butyrate have different rates of uptake and use.

steps.title: Opening the substrate
steps.text: Some community members unlock starches and fibres that others cannot digest.

steps.title: Microbes feed microbes
steps.text: Acetate-consuming butyrate producers can grow on products released by other bacteria.

steps.title: Where the products go
steps.text: Butyrate fuels the lining. Other fractions enter blood and are metabolised by the liver and wider body.

measurements.name: Stool SCFAs
measurements.text: The amount left after production, microbial use, absorption and transit. A stool concentration is not a production rate.

measurements.name: Isotope tracing
measurements.text: Labelled compounds reveal absorption and metabolic fate across compartments.

mechanisms.title: Tryptophan: indoles, immunity and kynurenine
mechanisms.lead: Tryptophan sits at a metabolic junction. Host cells and microbes send it into different routes with consequences for mucosal immunity and signalling.

nodes.name: Tryptophan
nodes.role: An amino acid supplied by dietary protein.

nodes.name: Microbial indoles
nodes.role: Microbial enzymes create chemically diverse indole derivatives.

nodes.name: AhR receptor
nodes.role: A chemical sensor activated by particular ligands.

nodes.name: IL-22 response
nodes.role: A cytokine pathway involved in epithelial defence.

nodes.name: Kynurenine pathway
nodes.role: Host IDO/TDO enzymes and microbial activities metabolise tryptophan along this branch.

nodes.name: Serotonin pathway
nodes.role: A separate branch supplies peripheral or brain serotonin synthesis.

steps.title: Making indoles
steps.text: Different microbes produce different tryptophan derivatives; indole-3-aldehyde is one experimentally traced example.

steps.title: A receptor connects chemistry to tissue
steps.text: Specific ligands engage AhR and change IL-22-linked mucosal responses.

steps.title: Competing metabolic branches
steps.text: Kynurenine metabolism involves host as well as microbial enzymes. Serotonin synthesis is another destination for the same precursor.

measurements.name: Metabolite panels
measurements.text: Measure particular indoles rather than treating all indole compounds as interchangeable.

measurements.name: Kynurenine / tryptophan
measurements.text: A ratio influenced by substrate availability and host inflammatory metabolism; it is not a direct readout of mood.

mechanisms.title: Vitamin B12: uptake and microbial competition
mechanisms.lead: B12 supports blood formation and the nervous system. Its human absorption route runs alongside a microbial economy of related cofactors.

nodes.name: Food B12
nodes.role: Digestion releases B12 from food proteins.

nodes.name: Intrinsic-factor complex
nodes.role: B12 binds intrinsic factor after earlier digestive binding steps.

nodes.name: Cubam uptake
nodes.role: Cubilin and amnionless enable uptake of the complex.

nodes.name: Host B12 supply
nodes.role: Absorbed B12 supports human enzyme reactions.

nodes.name: Microbial corrinoids
nodes.role: Some microbes synthesise B12 or related corrinoids.

nodes.name: Microbial importers
nodes.role: Other organisms rely on uptake and compete for available cofactors.

steps.title: The host absorption route
steps.text: Food B12 is released during digestion. Intrinsic factor, secreted by the stomach, carries B12 to the specialised uptake system in the terminal ileum.

steps.title: A microbial cofactor economy
steps.text: Mucus-associated partners can exchange corrinoids. Pseudovitamin B12 in a bacterial coculture supported microbial metabolism.

steps.title: Competition and location
steps.text: Microbial transport systems discriminate among corrinoids. Colonic production occurs downstream of the main human absorption site.

measurements.name: Blood B12
measurements.text: A circulating nutritional marker interpreted alongside symptoms and other laboratory findings.

measurements.name: Methylmalonic acid
measurements.text: Can reveal impaired B12-dependent metabolism; kidney function also influences the concentration.

links.title: Vitamin B12 — NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

mechanisms.title: Mucus: renewal, habitat and barrier
mechanisms.lead: The gut continually builds a living boundary. Mucus separates tissue from dense microbial populations while supplying habitat and food at its outer edge.

nodes.name: Goblet cells
nodes.role: Specialised epithelial cells secrete MUC2 mucin.

nodes.name: Inner mucus
nodes.role: A dense protective layer in the healthy colon.

nodes.name: Outer mucus
nodes.role: Expanded mucus creates a microbial habitat.

nodes.name: Mucin foragers
nodes.role: Organisms release and consume mucus-derived sugars.

nodes.name: Dietary fibre
nodes.role: An alternative source of microbial carbohydrates.

nodes.name: Epithelial surface
nodes.role: The cell layer underlying the mucus boundary.

steps.title: Building separation
steps.text: Secreted mucin forms structured layers that keep the densest bacterial populations away from the epithelium.

steps.title: Feeding at the boundary
steps.text: Microbes use glycans released from mucus. This ecology connects mucin foragers to other community members.

steps.title: Changing the food supply
steps.text: In fibre-deprived mice, greater mucus foraging eroded protection. Fibre availability changes the balance of substrates being consumed.

measurements.name: Mucus thickness and penetration
measurements.text: Microscopy and penetration assays describe the physical barrier; they differ from measuring a stool organism.

measurements.name: Faecal calprotectin
measurements.text: An intestinal inflammatory marker, rather than a direct measurement of mucus thickness or permeability.

mechanisms.title: Immune sensing: recognition and regulation
mechanisms.lead: The intestine samples microbial molecules continually. Some signals mobilise defence; others support regulation and long-term coexistence.

nodes.name: Bacterial molecules
nodes.role: Structures such as B. fragilis polysaccharide A reach host sensors.

nodes.name: TLR2 sensing
nodes.role: A receptor recognises particular microbial signals.

nodes.name: Regulatory T cells
nodes.role: These cells help regulate immune responses.

nodes.name: Butyrate
nodes.role: A fermentation product affects immune-cell differentiation.

nodes.name: Foxp3 regulation
nodes.role: Gene regulation supports regulatory T-cell identity.

nodes.name: Community combinations
nodes.role: Signals from several organisms can alter the combined cytokine response.

steps.title: Recognising a resident
steps.text: B. fragilis polysaccharide A can engage a regulatory immune pathway through TLR2.

steps.title: Metabolism reaches the nucleus
steps.text: Butyrate can influence chromatin at the Foxp3 locus and promote regulatory T-cell differentiation.

steps.title: Communities send combined signals
steps.text: Experiments with human intestinal isolates show that combined organisms can change dendritic-cell cytokine responses.

measurements.name: Cytokines and immune-cell populations
measurements.text: Assays identify particular signalling outputs and cell types; sample tissue and timing are part of the result.

measurements.name: Local metabolite exposure
measurements.text: Stool butyrate and the concentration experienced by tissue immune cells are different measurements.

mechanisms.title: Hydrogen: cross-feeding, methane and competing sinks
mechanisms.lead: Fermentation releases hydrogen. Other microbes consume it, changing which reactions remain favourable and which gases and metabolites accumulate.

nodes.name: Fermenting bacteria
nodes.role: Carbohydrate fermentation releases hydrogen and other products.

nodes.name: Hydrogen and formate
nodes.role: Electron-rich products pass between microbial partners.

nodes.name: Methanogenic archaea
nodes.role: Methanogens use suitable substrates to make methane.

nodes.name: Methane
nodes.role: Gas can leave in breath or intestinal gas.

nodes.name: Other hydrogen consumers
nodes.role: Acetogens and sulfate reducers provide competing routes.

nodes.name: Acetate or sulfide
nodes.role: Different consumers produce different end products.

steps.title: A shared resource
steps.text: Bacterial fermentation products can sustain methanogens. Defined cocultures show nutrient-dependent partnerships.

steps.title: Making methane
steps.text: Methanogenic archaea turn substrates into methane. Breath methane is associated with constipation and slower transit in clinical studies.

steps.title: Alternative destinations
steps.text: Hydrogen also feeds acetogenic and sulfate-reducing routes. Their relative activity depends on the community and local chemistry.

measurements.name: Breath hydrogen and methane
measurements.text: Gas concentrations reflect production, consumption, absorption and transit. They do not count bacterial or archaeal species.

measurements.name: Transit time
measurements.text: Measured passage through the gut helps distinguish a gas association from the process moving intestinal contents.

mechanisms.title: Movement: microbial chemistry, nerves and muscle
mechanisms.lead: Digestion depends on coordinated movement and secretion. Chemical sensors, enteric nerves, immune cells and smooth muscle form the control system.

nodes.name: Luminal chemicals
nodes.role: Nutrients and microbial metabolites stimulate host sensory cells.

nodes.name: Enterochromaffin cells
nodes.role: Chemical sensing triggers serotonin release.

nodes.name: Enteric neural circuits
nodes.role: Neural networks coordinate motor and secretory responses.

nodes.name: Smooth muscle and transit
nodes.role: Contraction patterns move and mix intestinal contents.

nodes.name: Muscularis macrophages
nodes.role: Immune cells signal to enteric neurons through BMP2.

nodes.name: Neuronal CSF1
nodes.role: Neurons provide a survival signal to local macrophages.

steps.title: Detecting the contents
steps.text: Enterochromaffin cells translate chemical cues into serotonin-mediated sensory signalling.

steps.title: Coordinating movement
steps.text: Microbiota-dependent serotonin signalling can change enteric neural development and transit in mice.

steps.title: A neuroimmune feedback loop
steps.text: Macrophages and enteric neurons exchange BMP2 and CSF1 signals. This loop links microbial stimuli to movement through a tissue support network.

measurements.name: Transit measurements
measurements.text: Whole-gut or regional passage time measures movement. Stool frequency alone does not describe every part of transit.

measurements.name: Manometry and secretion assays
measurements.text: Pressure patterns and fluid secretion measure distinct outputs of the control system.

mechanisms.title: Gut–brain communication: a two-way network
mechanisms.lead: The gut and brain continually exchange information. Nerves carry electrical messages, blood carries precursors and hormones, and microbial products shape immune and sensory responses.

nodes.name: Gut activity
nodes.role: Food, microbes, movement and host sensory cells generate several kinds of signals at once.

nodes.name: Sensory nerve fibres
nodes.role: Vagal and other sensory pathways carry information toward the central nervous system. Local serotonin can activate nerve receptors; neuropod cells can also signal through glutamate.

nodes.name: Brain networks
nodes.role: Incoming visceral information meets brain circuits involved in appetite, sensation, stress and behaviour. Brain serotonin is made locally from imported tryptophan.

nodes.name: Tryptophan availability
nodes.role: Tryptophan can cross the blood–brain barrier. Host and microbial metabolism influence its availability and its conversion into serotonin, kynurenine and indole-related products.

nodes.name: Immune and metabolic signals
nodes.role: Barrier biology, immune mediators and microbial metabolites connect gut activity with host responses. Their effects involve several intermediary cells and tissues.

nodes.name: Autonomic and stress output
nodes.role: Autonomic nerves and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal system change digestive conditions, including motor, secretory and immune activity.

steps.title: Neural communication
steps.text: Serotonin activates receptors on sensory nerve fibres. These fibres transmit electrical activity toward the brain. Separate neuropod-cell experiments identify a fast glutamate-mediated vagal circuit, adding another route from intestinal contents to the brainstem.

steps.title: A shared precursor
steps.text: Both gut and brain serotonin synthesis use dietary tryptophan. Its transport into the brain differs from serotonin movement. Microbial and host metabolism change the precursor landscape, including the kynurenine and indole branches.

steps.title: Immune communication
steps.text: Microbes influence intestinal immune responses and barrier function. Brain immune cells also respond to the microbial environment: experiments in mice connect microbial exposure and metabolites with microglial maturation.

steps.title: Metabolites and endocrine signals
steps.text: Short-chain fatty acids influence host cells and can participate in neuroimmune signalling. Enteroendocrine cells also translate nutrients and microbial products into neural and hormonal responses. Serotonin is one contributor within this wider chemical network.

steps.title: The return journey
steps.text: Brain output changes gut movement, secretion and immune activity through autonomic and hormonal control. Mouse colonisation experiments show that microbial exposure can also shape development of the hormonal stress response, linking the return path to the ecosystem it regulates.

measurements.name: Neural activity
measurements.text: Nerve recordings measure electrical responses; receptor experiments help identify which chemical signals produced them.

measurements.name: Precursor and metabolite pools
measurements.text: Blood tryptophan, kynurenine, tissue serotonin and microbial metabolites describe different pools. Their concentrations and rates of production answer different questions.

measurements.name: Immune and stress responses
measurements.text: Cytokines, immune-cell state, ACTH and glucocorticoids describe separate parts of the communication network. Mouse and human studies identify their experimental setting.
